source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 21 (PDF 169-186, printed 165-182); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 21 (Space and Environment), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 In this chapter, space refers to the region:

options.text: between the Earth's crust and core
beyond Earth's atmosphere where planets, stars and galaxies exist

blocks.explanation: Space is the region beyond Earth's atmosphere in which all celestial bodies exist and interact through gravity and electromagnetic radiations (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Space refers to a region beyond Earth's atmosphere in which all celestial bodies

blocks.prompt: 2 Environment is described as the surrounding conditions that are:
blocks.explanation: Environment is the surrounding physical, chemical and biological conditions in which living and non-living systems exist and interact (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Environment is the surrounding physical, chemical, and biological conditions

blocks.prompt: 3 The luminosity of a star is the:

options.text: total energy it emits per unit time as electromagnetic radiation
energy per unit area reaching the Earth
brightness of the star as seen from Earth
total energy it emits in its whole lifetime

blocks.explanation: Luminosity is the total amount of energy emitted by a star per unit time in the form of electromagnetic radiations (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Luminosity is the total amount of energy emitted by a star per unit time in the form of electromagnetic radiations

blocks.prompt: 4 The SI unit of luminosity is the:
blocks.explanation: Luminosity is a power, so it is measured in watts (21.1).

book_ref.quote: is measured in watts, indicating the total power of radiation emitted by a star

blocks.prompt: 5 Luminosity is the property that defines a star's:
blocks.explanation: Luminosity is a fundamental property that defines the intrinsic brightness of a star (21.1).

book_ref.quote: It is a fundamental property that defines the intrinsic brightness of a star

blocks.prompt: 6 The luminosity of a star primarily depends on its:
blocks.explanation: Luminosity depends mainly on the radius and the surface temperature of the star (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Luminosity of a star primarily depends on its radius and surface temperature

blocks.prompt: 7 Two stars have the same surface temperature. The larger one is more luminous because it has:

options.text: more surface area to emit radiation

blocks.explanation: Larger stars have more surface area to emit radiations and therefore tend to be more luminous (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Larger stars have more surface area to emit radiations and therefore, tend to be more luminous

blocks.prompt: 8 For two stars of equal size, the more luminous one is the star with the:
blocks.explanation: For stars of equal size, the one with the higher surface temperature radiates more energy and is more luminous (21.1).

book_ref.quote: for stars of equal size, the one with the higher surface temperature will radiate more energy

blocks.prompt: 9 The Stefan-Boltzmann law for a star of radius r and surface temperature T is:
blocks.explanation: Luminosity = surface area × radiant intensity = (4πr²)(σT⁴), Eq. (21.1).

book_ref.quote: The luminosity of a star can be represented as the product of its surface area (A=4πr²) and radiant intensity (I = σT⁴)

blocks.prompt: 10 According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the total output power of a star is proportional to its surface area and to:

options.text: the fourth power of its temperature
the square root of its temperature

blocks.explanation: The total output power is proportional to the product of surface area and the fourth power of temperature (21.1).

book_ref.quote: The total output power of a star is proportional to the product of its surface area and the fourth power of its temperature

blocks.prompt: 11 The value of the Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ is:
blocks.explanation: σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (21.1). 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K is Wien's constant and 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ is Hubble's constant.

book_ref.quote: Its value is 5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴

blocks.prompt: 12 If the surface temperature of a star is doubled while its radius stays the same, its luminosity becomes:
blocks.explanation: L ∝ T⁴, so L becomes 2⁴ = 16 times (21.1).

book_ref.quote: If a star becomes twice as hot, how many times more energy will it radiate?

blocks.prompt: 13 If the radius of a star is doubled at the same surface temperature, its luminosity becomes:
blocks.explanation: L ∝ r² at fixed T, so L becomes 2² = 4 times (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Larger stars have more surface area to emit radiations

blocks.prompt: 14 A star has twice the radius of another star but half its surface temperature. The ratio of its luminosity to that of the other star is:

book_ref.quote: Equation (21.1) is called Stefan-Boltzmann law

blocks.prompt: 15 The luminosity of the Sun is about:
blocks.explanation: The Sun shines with a luminosity of about 4 × 10²⁶ watts (21.1, Tidbit).

book_ref.quote: The Sun shines with an immense luminosity of about 4×10²⁶ watts

blocks.prompt: 16 A star has radius 6.0 × 10⁸ m and surface temperature 5000 K. Its luminosity is about (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴):

book_ref.quote: Using Stefan-Boltzmann law; L = 4πr² σ T⁴

blocks.prompt: 17 A star of luminosity 8.0 × 10²⁶ W has a surface temperature of 7000 K. Its radius is about:

book_ref.quote: The luminosity of a star is given as 2.5 × 10²⁶ W

blocks.prompt: 18 Radiant flux intensity of a star is the electromagnetic energy reaching the Earth's surface:

options.text: per unit area per unit time
per unit volume per unit time

blocks.explanation: Radiant flux intensity is the energy per unit area per unit time from a star that reaches the Earth's surface (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Radiant flux intensity is the amount of electromagnetic energy per unit area per unit time emitted from a star

blocks.prompt: 19 The SI unit of radiant flux intensity is:
blocks.explanation: Radiant flux intensity is luminosity per unit area, so its unit is W m⁻² (21.2).

book_ref.quote: radiant flux intensity is the luminosity per unit area measured on the surface of Earth

blocks.prompt: 20 Compared with the luminosity of a star, the radiant flux intensity received at the Earth is:

options.text: a small fraction of it (per square metre)

blocks.explanation: Radiant flux intensity is a small fraction of the total luminosity (21.2).

book_ref.quote: It is a small fraction of the total value of luminosity

blocks.prompt: 21 In F = L/4πr², the quantity r is:

options.text: the distance from the star to where the flux is measured

blocks.explanation: r is the distance from the star to the place of measurement; 4πr² is the area of the imaginary sphere over which the luminosity spreads (21.2, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: In F = L/4πr², r is the distance from the star to the place where the flux is measured

blocks.prompt: 22 For a star of constant luminosity, the radiant flux intensity F varies with distance r as:
blocks.explanation: F = L/4πr² with L constant, so F follows the inverse square law (21.2).

book_ref.quote: radiant flux intensity follows inverse square law with distance

blocks.prompt: 23 If the distance from a star is made four times, the radiant flux intensity becomes:
blocks.explanation: F ∝ 1/r², so at 4r the flux is 1/4² = 1/16 of its value (21.2).

book_ref.quote: when the distance from centre of a star is doubled (from r to 2r), intensity of the radiant flux reduces to one-fourth

blocks.prompt: 24 Moving to one-third of the original distance from a star makes the radiant flux intensity:
blocks.explanation: F ∝ 1/r²; at r/3 the flux is 3² = 9 times larger (21.2).

book_ref.quote: increasing the distance to three times its initial length (3r), decreases the flux by a factor of nine

blocks.prompt: 25 If the Earth were twice as far from the Sun, the sunlight reaching it would be:
blocks.explanation: By the inverse square law, doubling the distance makes the intensity one-fourth (21.2, Tidbit).

book_ref.quote: If Earth were twice as far from the Sun, the sunlight reaching it would be only one-fourth as intense

blocks.prompt: 26 Two stars give the same radiant flux at Earth, but star P is 5 times farther than star Q. The luminosity of P is:
blocks.explanation: Same F means L ∝ r², so L_P/L_Q = 5² = 25 (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Two stars appear equally bright in the night sky. However, one is 10 times farther away than the other.

blocks.prompt: 27 A star of luminosity 3.0 × 10²⁶ W is 2.0 × 10¹¹ m from a planet. The radiant flux intensity at the planet is about:

book_ref.quote: The luminosity of a star is 4.50 ×10²⁶ W

blocks.prompt: 28 The radiant flux from a star of luminosity 2.0 × 10²⁶ W is 500 W m⁻² at a planet. The distance of the planet from the star is about:

book_ref.quote: Radiant flux intensity from a star at a distance d is expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 29 The idea of standard candles began with the discovery that Cepheid variable stars:
blocks.explanation: In the 1910s Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that Cepheid variable stars pulse in a predictable way (21.2, Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that Cepheid variable stars pulse in a predictable way

blocks.prompt: 30 A standard candle is an astronomical object whose:
blocks.explanation: Standard candles are astronomical objects with known intrinsic brightness used to measure cosmic distances (21.3).

book_ref.quote: The standard candles are astronomical objects with known intrinsic brightness

blocks.prompt: 31 Comparing the known true brightness of a standard candle with its apparent brightness, astronomers find its distance using the:

options.text: law of conservation of angular momentum

blocks.explanation: Comparing apparent brightness with true brightness gives the distance through the inverse-square law of light (21.3).

book_ref.quote: astronomers can calculate its distance using the inverse-square law of light

blocks.prompt: 32 Which pair are examples of standard candles?

options.text: Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae

blocks.explanation: Examples of standard candles are Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae (21.3).

book_ref.quote: Examples of standard candles are Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae

blocks.prompt: 33 Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae are reliable distance indicators because they have:
blocks.explanation: Both have predictable luminosities, which makes them reliable distance indicators (21.3).

book_ref.quote: both of which have predictable luminosities that make them reliable distance indicators

blocks.prompt: 34 How bright a standard candle appears from the Earth is called its:
blocks.explanation: How bright a standard candle appears from the Earth is its apparent magnitude (21.3).

book_ref.quote: By comparing how bright a standard candle appears from the Earth (apparent magnitude)

blocks.prompt: 35 A Type Ia supernova of luminosity 5.0 × 10³⁵ W gives a flux of 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ W m⁻² at the Earth. Its distance is about:

book_ref.quote: measuring the distances to stars and galaxies is essential for understanding the structure and expansion of the universe

blocks.prompt: 36 Stars such as the Sun behave like:
blocks.explanation: Stars such as the Sun behave like blackbody radiators (21.4).

book_ref.quote: Stars such as Sun behave like blackbody radiator

blocks.prompt: 37 Stars generate their own energy due to:
blocks.explanation: Stars generate and emit their own energy due to nuclear fusion (21.4).

book_ref.quote: They generate and emit their own energy due to nuclear fusion

blocks.prompt: 38 The radiation emitted by a star covers a wide range of wavelengths and forms a:
blocks.explanation: Starlight forms a continuous spectrum without any gaps, similar to a blackbody spectrum (21.4).

book_ref.quote: forms a continuous spectrum without any gaps

blocks.prompt: 39 By studying the spectrum of a star, scientists can accurately estimate its:
blocks.explanation: By studying the spectrum, scientists can estimate the surface temperature of the star accurately (21.4).

book_ref.quote: By studying the spectrum, scientists can estimate the surface temperature of the star accurately

blocks.prompt: 40 According to Wien's displacement law, λmax of a blackbody is:

options.text: inversely proportional to its surface temperature
directly proportional to its surface temperature

blocks.explanation: λmax ∝ 1/T, i.e. λmax T = b (21.4, Eq. 21.3).

book_ref.quote: The wavelength corresponding to the radiation of maximum intensity emitted by a blackbody is inversely proportional to its surface temperature

blocks.prompt: 41 The value of Wien's constant b is:
blocks.explanation: Wien's constant b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K (21.4).

book_ref.quote: where b is a constant called Wien's constant whose value is 2.9 × 10⁻³ mK

blocks.prompt: 42 As the temperature of a blackbody increases, its λmax:
blocks.explanation: As T increases, λmax shifts towards shorter values (21.4).

book_ref.quote: as the temperature of a blackbody increases, the maximum wavelength of its emitted radiation shifts towards shorter values

blocks.prompt: 43 A star that appears blue or violet compared with a red star is:
blocks.explanation: Hotter objects emit radiation with shorter wavelengths (blue or violet); cooler ones appear red (21.4).

book_ref.quote: hotter objects emit radiation with shorter wavelengths (appearing blue or violet)

blocks.prompt: 44 Cooler objects emit radiation of maximum intensity at:
blocks.explanation: Cooler objects emit radiation with longer wavelengths, appearing red or infrared (21.4).

book_ref.quote: cooler objects emit radiation with longer wavelengths (appearing red or infrared)

blocks.prompt: 45 Star A has a shorter peak wavelength than star B. Therefore star A:
blocks.explanation: λmax ∝ 1/T, so a shorter peak wavelength means a higher surface temperature (21.4).

book_ref.quote: If a star's peak wavelength is shorter, what does that tell us about its temperature?

blocks.prompt: 46 The peak wavelength of radiation from a star is 400 nm. Its surface temperature is about (b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K):

book_ref.quote: This shift explains the change in colour of heated objects

blocks.prompt: 47 A star has a surface temperature of 10000 K. Its peak wavelength is (b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K):

book_ref.quote: Wien's Displacement law describes the relationship between the surface temperature T of a blackbody

blocks.prompt: 48 Star 1 at 5000 K has peak wavelength 600 nm. Star 2 has peak wavelength 400 nm. The temperature of star 2 is:

book_ref.quote: Another star has a peak wavelength of 320 nm

blocks.prompt: 49 If the absolute temperature of a blackbody is tripled, its λmax becomes:
blocks.explanation: λmax T = constant, so tripling T makes λmax one-third (21.4).

book_ref.quote: In simple words, hotter objects emit radiation

blocks.prompt: 50 By studying the emission and absorption spectra of a star, scientists can find:

options.text: the age of the universe directly
the elements the star is made of

blocks.explanation: Every star has its own light signature; its spectra show what elements it is made of (21.4, Tidbit).

book_ref.quote: by studying the emission and absorption spectra, scientists can determine what elements a star is made of

blocks.prompt: 51 The radiation from a heated (ideal) glowing body depends only on its:
blocks.explanation: This radiation depends only on the temperature of the object, not on its material or shape (21.4).

book_ref.quote: This radiation depends only on the temperature of the object, not on its material or shape

blocks.prompt: 52 As an object is heated more and more, its colour changes in the order:
blocks.explanation: With rising temperature the colour changes from dull red to bright yellow and then to white (21.4).

book_ref.quote: the colour of the object changes from dull red to bright yellow and then to white

blocks.prompt: 53 A blackbody is a body that:

options.text: reflects all radiation falling on it
absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits perfectly at all wavelengths

blocks.explanation: A blackbody absorbs all the radiations falling on it and also emits radiations at all wavelengths perfectly (21.4).

book_ref.quote: A blackbody is one that absorbs all the radiations falling on it and also emits radiations at all wavelengths perfectly

blocks.prompt: 54 Scientists use the idea of an ideal blackbody because real objects:

options.text: do not absorb or emit all radiation completely

blocks.explanation: Real objects do not absorb or emit all the radiation completely, which makes their behaviour hard to study (21.4).

book_ref.quote: real objects do not absorb or emit all the radiation completely

blocks.prompt: 55 A good practical example of a blackbody is:

options.text: a hollow cavity with a small hole and blackened inner walls

blocks.explanation: A hollow cavity with a small hole and blackened inner walls is a good example of a blackbody (21.4, Fig. 21.3).

book_ref.quote: a good example of a blackbody is a hollow cavity with a small hole and blackened inner walls

blocks.prompt: 56 The inner walls of a blackbody cavity are coated with:
blocks.explanation: The inner walls are coated with black carbon soot to absorb radiation effectively (21.4).

book_ref.quote: coated with black carbon soot to help them absorb radiation effectively

blocks.prompt: 57 Radiation entering the small hole of the cavity is absorbed because it:

options.text: bounces around inside and gets trapped
passes straight out of the other side
is reflected back through the hole at once

blocks.explanation: Radiation entering through the small hole bounces around inside and gets trapped (21.4).

book_ref.quote: When radiation enters through the small hole, it bounces around inside and gets trapped

blocks.prompt: 58 When the cavity is heated to a high enough temperature, the radiation it emits is called:
blocks.explanation: A heated cavity emits radiation of all wavelengths; this is blackbody radiation (21.4).

book_ref.quote: If the cavity is heated to a high enough temperature, it starts to emit radiation of all wavelengths

blocks.prompt: 59 On a graph of intensity against wavelength for a blackbody, raising the temperature:

options.text: lowers the curve and shifts its peak to longer wavelength
raises the curve and shifts its peak to shorter wavelength
makes the curve a straight line

blocks.explanation: As temperature increases the energy given off increases and the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths (21.4, Fig. 21.4).

book_ref.quote: the peak of the curve shifts to shorter wavelengths with rising temperature

blocks.prompt: 60 By Wien's law, the peak of the 2000 K blackbody curve lies at about:

book_ref.quote: the peaks lie at about 0.58, 0.72, 0.97 and 1.45 μm for 5000, 4000, 3000 and 2000 K

blocks.prompt: 61 Which of the following has an almost perfect blackbody spectrum?
blocks.explanation: The cosmic microwave background radiation has an almost perfect blackbody spectrum; a microwave oven's magnetron is not a blackbody source (21.4, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: It is the cosmic microwave background radiation that has an almost perfect blackbody spectrum

blocks.prompt: 62 Of two heated objects, one glows red-hot and the other white-hot. The hotter one is:

options.text: it cannot be said from colour

blocks.explanation: Colour changes from dull red to yellow to white as temperature rises, so the white-hot object is hotter (21.4).

book_ref.quote: One glows red-hot, and the other glows white-hot

blocks.prompt: 63 The radius of a star is calculated by using:

options.text: Hubble's law and the Coriolis effect
Wien's displacement law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law

blocks.explanation: The radius of a star can be calculated using Wien's displacement law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law (21.5).

book_ref.quote: The radius of a star can be calculated using Wien's displacement law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law

blocks.prompt: 64 In finding a star's radius, the first step is to find its surface temperature from:
blocks.explanation: The surface temperature T is first determined using Wien's displacement law (21.5).

book_ref.quote: the surface temperature T of a star is first determined using Wien's displacement law

blocks.prompt: 65 In finding a star's radius, its luminosity is obtained from the:

options.text: radiant flux intensity measured at Earth and the distance

blocks.explanation: The luminosity is calculated from the radiant flux intensity (L = 4πd²F) (21.5).

book_ref.quote: The Luminosity of a star can be calculated using the radiant flux intensity

blocks.prompt: 66 A star's peak wavelength is 580 nm and its luminosity is 1.8 × 10²⁶ W. Its radius is about (b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴):

book_ref.quote: then Stefan-Boltzmann law is used to determine the radius of star

blocks.text: 21.6 Emission and Absorption Spectra from Different Stars

blocks.prompt: 67 Stars emit a continuous spectrum because their surfaces are:

options.text: extremely hot and dense, like near-perfect blackbodies

blocks.explanation: Their extremely hot, dense surfaces behave like near-perfect blackbodies (21.6).

book_ref.quote: Stars emit a continuous spectrum of light because of their extremely hot, dense surfaces

blocks.prompt: 68 Atoms in a star's cooler outer atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths that correspond to:
blocks.explanation: Atoms absorb specific wavelengths corresponding to electronic transitions between energy levels (21.6).

book_ref.quote: atoms in the gaseous layers absorb specific wavelengths corresponding to electronic transitions between energy levels

blocks.prompt: 69 The dark lines in a star's continuous spectrum form its:
blocks.explanation: Dark lines where specific colours have been absorbed form the absorption spectrum (21.6).

book_ref.quote: This creates dark lines in the continuous spectrum

blocks.prompt: 70 Absorbed energy is re-emitted at the same wavelengths, yet dark lines are still seen because the re-emitted photons:

options.text: are scattered in various directions and seldom reach Earth
are all sent towards the Earth

blocks.explanation: Re-emitted photons are scattered in various directions, making them unlikely to reach observers on Earth (21.6).

book_ref.quote: the emitted photons are scattered in various directions making them unlikely to reach observers on Earth

blocks.prompt: 71 In spectra from distant galaxies, the lines appear at:

options.text: shorter wavelengths than their laboratory values
longer wavelengths than their laboratory values

blocks.explanation: The lines show an increase in wavelength from their known laboratory values: redshift (21.6).

book_ref.quote: the lines in the spectra show an increase in wavelength from their known laboratory values

blocks.prompt: 72 Redshift of light from distant galaxies occurs due to:

options.text: stretching of photons as they travel through the universe

blocks.explanation: Redshift occurs due to stretching of photons when they travel through the universe (21.6).

book_ref.quote: This phenomenon is called redshift which occurs due to stretching of photons

blocks.text: 21.7 Cosmic Redshift: Evidence for an Expanding Universe

blocks.prompt: 73 Cosmic redshift means light from distant galaxies is stretched towards the:
blocks.explanation: Cosmic redshift is light from distant galaxies stretched toward the red end of the spectrum (21.7).

book_ref.quote: Cosmic redshift refers to the effect in which light coming from distant galaxies across the universe is stretched toward the red end of the spectrum

blocks.prompt: 74 A more distant galaxy shows:

options.text: a larger redshift, so it is moving away faster

blocks.explanation: The greater the distance of a galaxy, the larger its redshift; it is moving away faster (21.7).

book_ref.quote: The greater the distance of a galaxy, the larger its redshift

blocks.prompt: 75 For speeds much less than c, the redshift Z is given by:
blocks.explanation: Z = Δλ/λ ≈ Δf/f ≈ v/c; the ratios are approximately equal, not 'much greater than' (21.7, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: Z = Δλ/λ ≈ Δf/f ≈ v/c (for speeds much less than c)

blocks.prompt: 76 A positive Δλ in light from a galaxy shows that the galaxy is:

options.text: at rest relative to the Earth

blocks.explanation: A positive Δλ indicates a redshift: the object is moving away from Earth (21.7).

book_ref.quote: When the observed change in wavelength Δλ is positive, it indicates a redshift (Z)

blocks.prompt: 77 A negative Δλ in the light from a star represents:

options.text: a redshift; the star is receding
a blue shift; the star is approaching the Earth
a rise in the star's temperature

blocks.explanation: A negative Δλ is a blue shift, showing the object is approaching the Earth (21.7).

book_ref.quote: a negative Δλ, represents a blue shift, showing that the object is approaching the Earth

blocks.prompt: 78 A spectral line of laboratory wavelength 500 nm is observed at 520 nm in a galaxy's light. The redshift Z is:

book_ref.quote: The observed change in the wavelength of light is directly related to the relative velocity between the source and the observer

blocks.prompt: 79 A galaxy shows a redshift Z = 0.04. Its recession speed is (take c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: By studying cosmic redshift, scientists can measure how fast the universe is expanding

blocks.prompt: 80 The redshift of galaxies is observed in all directions. This indicates that:

options.text: the Earth is at the centre of the universe

blocks.explanation: The redshift pattern observed in all directions indicates the expansion of the universe (21.7).

book_ref.quote: The redshift pattern is observed in all directions which indicates the expansion of the universe

blocks.prompt: 81 According to the chapter, galaxies appear to recede mainly because:

options.text: they are pushed by solar wind
the space between them is increasing

blocks.explanation: It is not just that galaxies move apart through space; the space between them is increasing (21.7).

book_ref.quote: rather, the space between them is increasing

blocks.prompt: 82 Cosmic redshift strongly supports the:

options.text: theory that stars do not emit energy

blocks.explanation: The redshift findings strongly support the Big Bang theory (21.7).

book_ref.quote: These findings strongly support the Big Bang theory

blocks.prompt: 83 Satellite remote sensing monitors Earth's environment using:
blocks.explanation: Satellite remote sensing uses sensors aboard orbiting spacecraft to monitor Earth's environment from space (21.8).

book_ref.quote: uses sensors aboard orbiting spacecraft to monitor and analyze Earth's environment from space

blocks.prompt: 84 Compared with ground-based methods, satellite remote sensing offers:

options.text: a single observation that cannot be repeated
wide geographic coverage and repeated observations

blocks.explanation: It offers wide geographic coverage and repeated observations over time (21.8).

book_ref.quote: it offers wide geographic coverage and repeated observations over time

blocks.prompt: 85 The first element of satellite remote sensing is:
blocks.explanation: The first and foremost element is the source or illumination, which illuminates the target with electromagnetic radiation (21.8).

book_ref.quote: The first and foremost element of SRS is source or illumination

blocks.prompt: 86 In remote sensing, the interaction of radiation with the atmosphere may be in the form of:
blocks.explanation: After leaving the source, radiation interacts with the atmosphere by scattering, reflection etc. (21.8).

book_ref.quote: This interaction may be in the form of scattering, reflection etc.

blocks.prompt: 87 In remote sensing, the sensors that record radiation from the target are:

options.text: not in contact with the target

blocks.explanation: The emitted or reflected radiations are recorded by sensors which are remote (not in contact with target) (21.8).

book_ref.quote: recorded by sensors which are remote (not in contact with target)

blocks.prompt: 88 The last step of satellite remote sensing is:
blocks.explanation: The last step is interpretation and analysis: the processed image is interpreted electronically or digitally (21.8).

book_ref.quote: The processed image is then interpreted (to get information) electronically or digitally

blocks.prompt: 89 Hubble's law states that the recession velocity of a galaxy is:

options.text: proportional to the square of its distance
directly proportional to its distance from Earth

book_ref.quote: The recession velocity v of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance d from the Earth

blocks.prompt: 90 The value of Hubble's constant given in the chapter is:

book_ref.quote: Hₒ is called Hubble's constant and its value is 2.3×10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 91 On a graph of recession velocity against distance of galaxies, the slope gives:
blocks.explanation: The graph is linear and its slope corresponds to the Hubble constant H₀ (21.8, Fig. 21.6).

book_ref.quote: The slope of this linear trend corresponds to the Hubble constant (H₀)

blocks.prompt: 92 A galaxy is at a distance of 1.0 × 10²⁴ m. Its recession velocity is (H₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: the farther a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away

blocks.prompt: 93 A galaxy recedes at 1.5 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Its distance is about (H₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: Edwin Hubble established the foundation for modern cosmology

blocks.prompt: 94 Galaxy X recedes three times as fast as galaxy Y. By Hubble's law, galaxy X is:

options.text: nine times as far as Y
three times as far as Y
at the same distance as Y

blocks.explanation: v = H₀d, so v ∝ d: three times the speed means three times the distance (21.8).

book_ref.quote: A galaxy is moving away from us very fast. According to Hubble's Law, what does that tell us about its distance?

blocks.prompt: 95 An observer in another galaxy would see:

options.text: the other galaxies moving away from him too

blocks.explanation: All galaxies are moving away from each other; an observer in another galaxy will observe the same effect (21.8).

book_ref.quote: An observer in another galaxy will observe the same effect

blocks.prompt: 96 In the inflated-balloon model of the expanding universe, the dots on the balloon represent:
blocks.explanation: The dots on the surface of the balloon represent the galaxies (21.8, Fig. 21.7).

book_ref.quote: The dots which are marked on the surface of a balloon represent the galaxies

blocks.prompt: 97 The balloon model shows that the expansion of the universe:

options.text: has its centre at the Earth
happens everywhere and has no special centre

blocks.explanation: No matter where we are, galaxies move away; the expansion is everywhere with no special centre (21.8).

book_ref.quote: This means the expansion is happening everywhere, and there is no special centre

blocks.prompt: 98 Reversing the expansion of the universe in time implies that, far in the past, all matter was:

options.text: spread over a very large cold volume
compressed into a very small, dense and hot state
made only of galaxies far apart

blocks.explanation: Going further back, all matter was compressed into a very small, dense and hot state (21.8).

book_ref.quote: all matter was compressed into a very small, dense, and hot state

blocks.prompt: 99 According to the Big Bang theory, the universe began about:
blocks.explanation: The Big Bang theory proposes the universe began from an initial singularity about 13.8 billion years ago (21.8).

book_ref.quote: the universe began from an initial singularity about 13.8 billion years ago

blocks.prompt: 100 Before Hubble's discovery, most scientists thought the universe was:
blocks.explanation: Before Hubble's discovery most scientists thought the universe was static (21.8, Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: Before Hubble's discovery, most scientists thought the universe was static

blocks.prompt: 101 Earth's climate system is described as:

options.text: the weather of a single day
the long-term pattern of temperature, rainfall, wind and weather in a region

blocks.explanation: Earth's climate system is a long-term pattern of temperature, rainfall, wind and other weather conditions in a region (21.9).

book_ref.quote: Earth's climate system is a long-term pattern of temperature, rainfall, wind, and other weather conditions in a region

blocks.prompt: 102 The number of components in Earth's climate system is:
blocks.explanation: The climate system is made up of five components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere and biosphere (21.9).

book_ref.quote: The climate system of Earth is made up of five components

blocks.prompt: 103 The cryosphere component of the climate system consists of:
blocks.explanation: The cryosphere is ice and permafrost (21.9).

book_ref.quote: the cryosphere (ice and permafrost)

blocks.prompt: 104 Earth's upper rocky layer is called the:
blocks.explanation: The lithosphere is Earth's upper rocky layer (21.9).

book_ref.quote: the lithosphere (Earth's upper rocky layer)

blocks.prompt: 105 Which of the following is NOT one of the five components of Earth's climate system?
blocks.explanation: The five components are atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere and biosphere; the magnetosphere is not listed (21.9).

book_ref.quote: These components work together and affect each other

blocks.prompt: 106 Human activities that shape the climate, named in the chapter, are:

options.text: burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests

blocks.explanation: Climate is shaped by natural factors (Sun, ocean currents) and human activities such as burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests (21.9).

book_ref.quote: human activities, such as burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests

blocks.prompt: 107 Surface ocean currents are mostly caused by:
blocks.explanation: Surface currents are mostly caused by wind pushing water across the ocean's top layer (21.10).

book_ref.quote: Surface currents are mostly caused by wind

blocks.prompt: 108 The vertical circulation of seawater is called:
blocks.explanation: The vertical circulation of water is called thermohaline circulation (21.10).

book_ref.quote: The vertical circulation of water is called thermohaline circulation

blocks.prompt: 109 Large circular ocean current systems shaped by the Earth's rotation are called:
blocks.explanation: The rotation of the Earth creates large circular current systems known as gyres (21.10).

book_ref.quote: creating large circular current systems known as gyres

blocks.prompt: 110 Ocean gyres in the southern hemisphere spin:
blocks.explanation: Gyres spin clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern hemisphere (21.10).

book_ref.quote: These spin clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern hemisphere

blocks.prompt: 111 Wind patterns on Earth are created due to:

options.text: uneven heating of the Earth's surface

blocks.explanation: Wind patterns are created due to uneven heating of the Earth's surface; warm air rises and cooler air moves in (21.10).

book_ref.quote: Wind patterns are created due to an uneven heating of the Earth's surface

blocks.prompt: 112 Which set lists the wind belts named in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Uneven heating forms wind belts like trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies (21.10).

book_ref.quote: forming distinct wind belts like trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies

blocks.prompt: 113 Ocean currents help regulate the planet's climate because they:

options.text: carry warm water poleward and bring cold water back
carry cold water to the equator only
move water only at the poles

blocks.explanation: Currents move warm water from the equator toward the poles and bring cold water back (21.10).

book_ref.quote: The currents move warm water from the equator toward the poles and bring cold water back

blocks.text: 21.11 Global Climate and Energy Transfer from the Sun

blocks.prompt: 114 The main source of energy that produces changes in the global climate is:
blocks.explanation: Energy received from the Sun plays an important role in producing changes in the global climate (21.11).

book_ref.quote: Energy received from the Sun plays a important role in producing changes in the global climate

blocks.prompt: 115 Earth's energy budget is the balance between:

options.text: energy of the Sun and the Moon
heat of oceans and heat of land
solar energy absorbed by the Earth and energy it radiates back into space
energy of trade winds and westerlies

blocks.explanation: The energy budget is the balance between solar energy absorbed and energy radiated back into space (21.11).

book_ref.quote: The Earth's energy budget refers to the balance between the solar energy absorbed by the Earth and the energy it radiates back into space

blocks.prompt: 116 When the Earth is colder and more ice and snow cover the surface, the Earth becomes even cooler because ice and snow:

options.text: are bright and reflect much sunlight back into space

blocks.explanation: Ice and snow are bright and reflect a large amount of sunlight back into space, making the Earth cooler (21.11).

book_ref.quote: Ice and snow are bright and reflect a large amount of sunlight back into space

blocks.prompt: 117 When ice melts and exposes land and ocean, the Earth warms further because these darker surfaces:

options.text: absorb more sunlight and reflect less

blocks.explanation: Darker surfaces like land and oceans absorb more sunlight and reflect less, so the Earth becomes warmer (21.11).

book_ref.quote: This exposes darker surfaces like land and oceans, which absorb more sunlight and reflect less

blocks.prompt: 118 Energy from the Sun is balanced by energy leaving the Earth in the form of:
blocks.explanation: Incoming solar energy is balanced by outgoing infrared (heat) radiation from the Earth (21.11).

book_ref.quote: The energy coming in from the Sun is balanced by the energy going out from Earth in the form of infrared (heat) radiation

blocks.prompt: 119 Global warming results because greenhouse gases:

options.text: trap infrared radiation and stop it escaping to space

blocks.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap infrared radiations, preventing them from escaping into space, so the Earth warms (21.11).

book_ref.quote: greenhouse gases trap infrared radiations, preventing it from escaping into space

blocks.prompt: 120 The fraction of the Sun's energy absorbed by the Earth is about:
blocks.explanation: The Earth absorbs about 70% of the Sun's energy; the rest is reflected by clouds, ice and deserts (21.11, Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: The Earth only absorbs about 70% of the Sun's energy

blocks.prompt: 121 At the equator, direct intense sunlight causes warm air to rise, forming:
blocks.explanation: Direct intense sunlight at the equator makes warm air rise and form low-pressure zones (21.11).

book_ref.quote: The equator receives direct, intense sunlight, causing warm air to rise and form low-pressure zones

blocks.prompt: 122 At the poles, slanted weaker sunlight leads to:

options.text: warm, rising air and low-pressure zones
cold, sinking air and high-pressure zones

blocks.explanation: The poles get slanted, weaker sunlight, leading to cold, sinking air and high-pressure zones (21.11).

book_ref.quote: the poles get slanted, weaker sunlight, leading to cold, sinking air and high-pressure zones

blocks.prompt: 123 The equator is heated more than the poles because:

options.text: the poles are nearer to the Sun
the equator receives direct sunlight while the poles receive oblique sunlight

blocks.explanation: The equator receives direct sunlight while the poles receive oblique sunlight at an angle, resulting in uneven heating (21.11, Fig. 21.13).

book_ref.quote: while the poles receive oblique sunlight at an angle, resulting in uneven heating

blocks.prompt: 124 Global atmospheric circulation is driven by:

options.text: the energy imbalance between the equator and the poles
the salt in the oceans alone

blocks.explanation: The energy imbalance between equator and poles drives global atmospheric circulation (21.11).

book_ref.quote: This energy imbalance drives global atmospheric circulation

blocks.prompt: 125 Specific angular momentum of an air mass is:

options.text: angular momentum per unit mass, L = rv

blocks.explanation: Specific angular momentum is the angular momentum per unit mass: L = rv (21.12, Eq. 21.6).

book_ref.quote: we usually consider specific angular momentum, which is the angular momentum per unit mass

blocks.prompt: 126 In L = mvr for an air mass, r is:

options.text: its distance from the Earth's rotation axis

blocks.explanation: r is the distance of the air mass from the Earth's rotation axis (21.12).

book_ref.quote: The angular momentum of an air mass about Earth's rotation axis is given by L = mvr

blocks.prompt: 127 An air mass moves so that its distance from the rotation axis falls from 6.0 × 10⁶ m to 4.0 × 10⁶ m. If its speed was 400 m s⁻¹, its new speed (rv constant) is:

book_ref.quote: As the air mass moves, r decreases and so v increases to keep rv constant

blocks.prompt: 128 The apparent deflection of moving air due to Earth's rotation is called the:
blocks.explanation: The apparent deflection of moving air due to Earth's rotation is called the Coriolis effect (21.12).

book_ref.quote: this type of effect is called Coriolis Effect

blocks.prompt: 129 In the northern hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air:
blocks.explanation: The deflection is toward the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere (21.12).

book_ref.quote: The deflection occurs toward right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere

blocks.prompt: 130 The Coriolis deflection of moving air:

options.text: changes its speed but not its path
changes its path but not its speed

blocks.explanation: The deflection does not affect the speed of the air but changes its path, creating curved wind patterns (21.12).

book_ref.quote: This deflection does not affect the speed of the air but changes its path

blocks.prompt: 131 The three atmospheric circulation cells in each hemisphere are:
blocks.explanation: Deflected air flows form three cells in each hemisphere: the Hadley cell, Ferrel cell and Polar cell (21.12, Fig. 21.14).

book_ref.quote: the Hadley cell, Ferrel cell, and Polar cell

blocks.prompt: 132 Air moving from the equator toward a pole keeps rv constant. Compared with the ground beneath it, it:

options.text: moves eastward faster and runs ahead
moves at exactly the same speed

blocks.explanation: r decreases so v increases; the ground at higher latitude turns more slowly, so this air runs ahead (deflected east). It is pole-to-equator air that lags behind (21.12, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: It is air moving from a pole toward the equator that lags behind the faster-moving surface

blocks.text: 21.13 Role of Salt and Density in Ocean Circulation

blocks.prompt: 133 The amount of salt in ocean water is called:
blocks.explanation: The amount of salt in ocean water is called salinity (21.13).

book_ref.quote: The amount of salt in ocean water is called salinity

blocks.prompt: 134 Salty water is denser because dissolved salt:

options.text: increases the mass without much increase in volume

blocks.explanation: Dissolved salt increases the mass of the water without significantly increasing its volume, so density rises (21.13).

book_ref.quote: the dissolved salt increases the mass of the water without significantly increasing its volume

blocks.prompt: 135 Which seawater is the densest?
blocks.explanation: Cold water is denser than warm, and salty water denser than less salty, so cold salty water is densest (21.13).

book_ref.quote: Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than less salty water

blocks.prompt: 136 Surface waters become colder and saltier and sink, often due to:

options.text: evaporation or the formation of sea ice

blocks.explanation: Surface waters become colder and saltier, often due to evaporation or sea-ice formation, become denser and sink (21.13).

book_ref.quote: When surface waters become colder and saltier often due to evaporation or the formation of sea ice

blocks.prompt: 137 Deep ocean circulation transports around the globe:

options.text: heat and gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide

blocks.explanation: Deep circulation helps transport heat and gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) around the globe (21.13).

book_ref.quote: This deep circulation helps transport heat, and gases (such as oxygen and carbon dioxide)

blocks.prompt: 138 Thermohaline circulation is often called the:
blocks.explanation: Thermohaline circulation is often referred to as the global conveyor belt (21.14).

book_ref.quote: often referred to as the global conveyor belt

blocks.prompt: 139 Thermohaline circulation is driven by variations in:
blocks.explanation: It is driven by variations in water temperature and salinity, which together affect density (21.14).

book_ref.quote: This circulation is driven by variations in water temperature and salinity

blocks.prompt: 140 In thermohaline circulation, warm, less dense water near the equator:

options.text: moves along the ocean floor to the poles
moves along the surface toward the polar regions

blocks.explanation: Warm, less dense water near the equator moves along the surface toward the poles, carrying heat (21.14).

book_ref.quote: Warm, less dense water near the equator moves along the surface toward the polar regions

blocks.prompt: 141 In polar areas, water sinks in thermohaline circulation because:

options.text: it cools and its salinity rises from sea-ice formation, making it denser
it warms and becomes less dense

blocks.explanation: In polar areas water cools and becomes denser due to lower temperature and increased salinity from sea-ice formation, so it sinks (21.14).

book_ref.quote: increased salinity from sea ice formation, causing it to sink

blocks.prompt: 142 One full cycle of the global conveyor belt takes approximately:
blocks.explanation: The global conveyor belt takes approximately 1,000 years to cycle water through all ocean basins (21.14).

book_ref.quote: takes approximately 1,000 years to cycle water

blocks.prompt: 143 In the figure of thermohaline circulation, the red ribbons represent:
blocks.explanation: Warm surface currents (red ribbons) flow poleward; sinking cold water is shown by blue ribbons (21.14, Fig. 21.15).

book_ref.quote: warm surface currents (represented by red ribbons) flow poleward

blocks.prompt: 144 According to the chapter, if global warming slows down thermohaline circulation:

options.text: the whole Earth would freeze at once
Europe could face a mini-ice age
the oceans would stop being salty

blocks.explanation: If global warming slows it down, Europe could face a mini-ice age even while the rest of the world heats up (21.14, Tidbit).

book_ref.quote: If global warming slows it down, Europe could face a mini-ice age
